title: Sophia Girls Academy: More Than Just an Educational Platform
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Learn how Sophia Girls Academy was founded and how it is helping girls access educational opportunities around the world.

content.text: Not everyone grows up with the same opportunities. For many girls living in rural areas, finding information about scholarships, universities, or even someone to ask for advice can be difficult. Sophia Girls Academy was created to help change that.
How It Started
Sophia Girls Academy was founded by Bakdana and her friend Azhar. She knew how challenging it could be to find educational opportunities and prepare for exams.

Together, they created Sophia Girls Academy to provide free education, mentorship, and academic support for girls around the world. Their goal is simple: to help every girl reach her potential, no matter where she comes from.
Our Mission

Our goal is to support girls from rural areas by giving them access to educational and professional opportunities. We help students learn about scholarships, university admissions, international programs, and important exams while also teaching practical skills they can use in their studies and future careers.
More than anything, we want to build a community where ambitious girls can learn, grow, and support one another.
What We Offer

items: Basic Technical Skills (Excel, Word, and PowerPoint)

content.text: Whether you're looking to improve your grades, prepare for university, or simply learn something new, there's a place for you here.
How the Program Works

The program officially starts on July 1. Students join WhatsApp groups based on the tracks they choose. Some mentors offer individual sessions through Calendly, while others teach through group lessons, workshops, and webinars.
Every two weeks, participants complete a short feedback form so we can continue improving the learning experience for everyone.

Sophia Girls Academy is more than an educational program. It’s a community that believes every girl deserves the chance to reach her full potential. No matter where you come from, your future should be shaped by your ambitions, not by your location.

title: The Woman Who Founded One of the World’s Oldest Universities
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Learn about Fatima al-Fihri, the woman who founded one of the world’s oldest universities over 1,000 years ago, and how her story continues to inspire girls today.

content.text: When people hear the word university, they usually think of places like Oxford or Harvard. But did you know that one of the world’s oldest universities was founded by a woman over 1,100 years ago?
Her name was Fatima al-Fihri, and surprisingly, not many people know her story.
Who Was Fatima al-Fihri?

Fatima was born in the 9th century and later moved with her family to Fez, Morocco. Her father was a successful businessman who believed that education was important. After his death, Fatima and her sister inherited his wealth.
Many people would have spent that money on themselves, but Fatima had a different idea. She wanted to create something that would help people not only then, but in the future as well.
A Place Where Anyone Could Learn

In 859, Fatima used her inheritance to build a mosque. Over time, it became a place where people came not only to pray but also to study. It later grew into the University of al-Qarawiyyin, which is recognized as one of the oldest universities still operating today.

Students studied mathematics, astronomy, languages, medicine, philosophy, and many other subjects. People traveled from different places to learn there, and the university continued to grow for centuries.
Why Is Her Story Important?

When we talk about history, we often hear the names of scientists, inventors, or political leaders. But people like Fatima al-Fihri are just as important. She didn’t invent a new technology or make a scientific discovery. Instead, she created a place where thousands of people could learn.

Education gives people opportunities. It helps them build careers, solve problems, and improve their communities. Fatima understood that more than a thousand years ago, and her idea is still relevant today.
What Can We Learn From Her?
Fatima al-Fihri’s story shows that making a difference doesn’t always mean standing in the spotlight. Sometimes, creating opportunities for others has an even bigger impact.

At Sophia Girls Academy, we believe in the same idea. Every girl deserves access to education, support, and the chance to reach her goals. Fatima’s story reminds us that investing in education can change lives—not just for one person, but for generations to come.

title: The Woman Who Dared to Say Women Deserved More
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Discover how Margaret Fuller became one of the earliest voices advocating for women's education, equality, and the freedom to choose their own paths.

content.text: In July 1843, an essay called The Great Lawsuit was published in The Dial magazine. Today, many people consider it one of the first feminist works in American history. The woman behind it was Margaret Fuller.
Although her name isn’t as well known as many other historical figures, her ideas helped start important conversations about women’s rights and education.
Who Was Margaret Fuller?

Margaret Fuller was an American writer, editor, and journalist. At a time when women were expected to focus only on their homes and families, she believed they should also have access to education, meaningful careers, and the freedom to make their own choices.

She loved learning from a young age and spent years studying literature, history, philosophy, and different languages. Education became a big part of her life, and she wanted other women to have the same opportunities.
The Essay That Started a Conversation

In 1843, Fuller published The Great Lawsuit in The Dial, a literary magazine where she worked as an editor. In her essay, she argued that women should not be limited by society’s expectations. Instead, they should be able to learn, grow, and choose their own paths.
A few years later, she expanded these ideas into a book called Woman in the Nineteenth Century. It became one of the most influential early feminist books in the United States.
Why Does It Still Matter?
Today, it may seem normal for girls to go to school, attend university, and build careers in any field they choose. But in the 19th century, these opportunities were far from guaranteed.
Margaret Fuller believed that education gives people the freedom to think for themselves. She encouraged women to ask questions, develop their talents, and believe that their voices mattered.
Looking Back

More than 180 years have passed since The Great Lawsuit was first published, but its message is still relevant today. Around the world, many girls are still working to gain equal access to education and opportunities.

At Sophia Girls Academy, we believe in the same idea Margaret Fuller shared many years ago: every girl deserves the chance to learn, grow, and build the future she wants. Sometimes, real change begins with one person who is willing to speak up.

title: The Woman Who Founded a Political Party Before Women Could Even Vote
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Discover how Nezihe Muhiddin challenged social expectations by founding a political party for women before they even had the right to vote.

content.text: Imagine starting a political party when women weren’t even allowed to vote.

It sounds impossible, but that’s exactly what Nezihe Muhiddin tried to do in July 1923. While many people know about the women who later gained the right to vote in Turkey, far fewer know about the woman who helped start that conversation.
Who Was Nezihe Muhiddin?

Nezihe Muhiddin was a Turkish writer, teacher, and women’s rights activist. She believed that women should have the same opportunities as men, not only in education but also in public life and politics.
She spent years writing articles and books about women’s rights. However, writing wasn’t enough for her. She wanted to see real change.
A Bold Idea

In July 1923, Nezihe Muhiddin and a group of women founded the People’s Party of Women. Their goal was simple: they wanted women to have a voice in politics and take part in decisions that affected their lives.
There was one problem. At that time, women in Turkey didn’t have the right to vote or run for office. Because of this, the party was never officially recognized.
Even though the project did not succeed, Nezihe Muhiddin refused to give up.
Continuing The Fight

Instead of stopping, she helped establish the Turkish Women’s Union, an organization that continued working for women’s rights. The union encouraged women to become more involved in education, public life, and social issues.

Years later, in 1934, Turkish women gained the right to vote and run for parliament. Although many people remember this achievement, fewer remember those who had been fighting for it long before it became reality.
Why Does Her Story Matter?
Change rarely happens overnight. Before new laws are passed, someone has to ask difficult questions and imagine a different future.
Nezihe Muhiddin was one of those people. She believed that women deserved more opportunities and that education, leadership, and equal participation in society should not depend on gender.
Looking Back

Today, girls can study, build careers, and become leaders in ways that once seemed impossible. These opportunities exist because people like Nezihe Muhiddin were willing to challenge the expectations of their time.
Her name may not appear in every history book, but her work helped open doors for future generations. And sometimes, that’s exactly how real change begins.
Credits
• Photo Source: Sanat Karavani

title: The Woman Who Refused to Wait for Equality
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Discover how Emmeline Pankhurst fought for women's suffrage and became a symbol of the women's rights movement.

content.text: Imagine being told that your opinion doesn’t matter simply because you’re a woman. Today, it sounds unfair. But in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, that was the reality for millions of women in the United Kingdom. They couldn’t vote, and they had almost no say in the decisions that shaped their lives.
One woman decided that staying silent was no longer an option. Her name was Emmeline Pankhurst.
Who Was Emmeline Pankhurst?
Emmeline Pankhurst was born on July 14, 1858, in Manchester, England. From a young age, she was interested in politics and believed that women deserved the same rights as men.
As she grew older, she realized that talking about change wasn’t enough. If women wanted equal rights, someone had to take action.
A Movement That Changed History

In 1903, Emmeline founded the Women’s Social and Political Union (WSPU). Unlike many other organizations at the time, the WSPU believed in taking bold action to bring attention to women’s suffrage, the right to vote.
Its members organized marches, gave speeches, held protests, and refused to stay quiet. Their actions were often criticized, and many women, including Emmeline herself, were arrested more than once.
Even while in prison, she continued fighting for what she believed in.
Why Did She Keep Going?
For Emmeline, the fight was never just about voting. She believed that if women had no voice in politics, they would continue to have fewer opportunities in education, work, and everyday life.
She wanted girls to grow up knowing that their opinions mattered and that they had the right to shape their own future.
A Lasting Impact
In 1918, some women in the United Kingdom gained the right to vote. Ten years later, women finally received voting rights on the same terms as men.
Emmeline Pankhurst did not live to see that final change, but her work helped make it possible.

Today, many of the opportunities women have are the result of people who refused to accept that things could never change. Emmeline Pankhurst was one of those people. Her story reminds us that progress often begins with someone who is willing to stand up, speak out, and believe that a better future is possible.
Credits
• Photo Source: Pankhurst Museum

title: She Chose to Fight for a Future She Would Never See
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Learn about Qiu Jin, a Chinese revolutionary who fought for women's rights and education.

content.text: Some people change history by making discoveries. Others do it by speaking up when almost everyone else stays silent.
Qiu Jin was one of those people.

She dreamed of a future where women could study, choose their own path, and have the same opportunities as men. At the beginning of the 20th century, those ideas were considered radical in China. But that didn’t stop her from fighting for them.
More Than a Writer

Qiu Jin was born in 1875 in China. As a child, she received an education, something that many girls at the time never had the chance to experience. She loved reading and writing, but she also believed that education should lead to action.

Later, she moved to Japan, where she continued her studies and met people who shared her dream of changing China. During this time, she became more involved in politics and started writing about women’s rights, equality, and the future of her country.
Speaking Up for Women
Qiu Jin believed that women should not be limited to traditional roles. She encouraged girls to get an education, become independent, and make their own decisions about their lives.

Through her articles, speeches, and poetry, she challenged ideas that had existed for generations. She knew that changing people’s minds would not be easy, but she believed every voice could make a difference.
A Price She Was Willing to Pay
Qiu Jin also joined the movement against the Qing government. She believed that political change and equal opportunities for women were connected.
In 1907, after a planned uprising failed, she was arrested. Even during questioning, she refused to reveal information about others involved in the movement.
On July 15, 1907, Qiu Jin was executed. She was only 31 years old.
Why Do We Still Remember Her?
Qiu Jin never saw the future she hoped for. She never saw girls attending universities, becoming leaders, or having more freedom to choose their own path.
But her ideas lived on.

Today, she is remembered not only as a revolutionary, but also as a writer who believed education could help build a better future. Her story reminds us that real change often begins with people who are willing to speak up, even when it is difficult.
More than a century later, her message is still relevant: every girl deserves the chance to learn, to dream, and to decide her own future.

• Photo Source: Think Magazine

title: The Women Who Refused to Stay Silent
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Learn about the 20,000 women who marched against apartheid pass laws in South Africa in 1956.

content.text: Imagine thousands of women walking through the streets of Pretoria, knowing exactly why they are there. No social media. No cameras everywhere. No hashtag that could make their message travel around the world in seconds. Just people, signs, petitions, and a shared feeling that something had to change.

This is what happened on August 9, 1956, when around 20,000 women marched to the Union Buildings in Pretoria, South Africa. They were protesting against apartheid pass laws that required Black South Africans to carry passes that controlled where they could live and work and restricted their movement.
For these women, this wasn’t some distant political issue. It was about their everyday lives, their families, and their freedom.
20,000 Voices, One Message

The women came from different communities and backgrounds. They weren’t all politicians or famous activists. Many were simply women who had decided that they couldn’t just watch what was happening around them.

They brought petitions containing more than 100,000 signatures and delivered them to the government. Then came one of the most memorable parts of the protest: the women stood in silence for 30 minutes.
And honestly, I think that might be one of the most powerful details of the whole story.

We usually imagine protests as loud. People shouting, signs everywhere, speeches, cameras. But imagine 20,000 people standing together without saying a word. Sometimes silence isn’t the absence of a message. Sometimes, it is the message.
You Don’t Have to Be Powerful to Make a Difference
Something about this story feels especially relevant today.

We often think that making a difference requires having a huge platform. You need thousands of followers, a big organization, or some important title next to your name. Social media can make it feel like your voice doesn’t matter unless hundreds of people are listening.
But the women of 1956 didn’t start with any of that.
They had something much simpler: each other.
One person speaking up can be ignored. But when thousands of people stand together, ignoring them becomes much harder.
And I think that’s one of the biggest lessons from this march. You don’t have to already be powerful to create change. Sometimes, people become powerful because they choose to stand together.
Why We Still Remember August 9
Today, August 9 is celebrated as National Women’s Day in South Africa. It is a day to remember the women who marched in 1956 and the courage it took for them to challenge apartheid.
But I don’t think we should remember them only as a group of women from a history textbook.
They were people who had normal lives. They had families, responsibilities, fears, and probably plenty of reasons to stay home. And yet, they showed up.
That’s what makes their story feel real to me.

They didn’t know whether their protest would become a national symbol decades later. They weren’t thinking about how history would describe them. They simply knew that something was wrong and they decided to do something about it.
What Does Their March Mean Today?
More than seventy years later, the world is obviously different. But the question behind their march is still worth asking: What do we do when we see something that isn’t right?
It is easy to believe that someone else will speak first. Someone more experienced. Someone louder. Someone with a bigger platform.
But change rarely begins with everyone being ready.
It begins with someone taking the first step.
And on August 9, 1956, around 20,000 women took that step together.
Maybe that’s why their story has lasted.
Not because they were untouchable heroes, but because they were ordinary people who decided that being ordinary didn’t mean being powerless.
Sometimes, history isn’t made by the people who have the biggest voices.
Sometimes, it’s made by the people who simply refuse to stay silent.
Credits
• Photo Source: VectorStock

title: Bertha Lutz: The Woman Who Refused to Wait
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Learn about Bertha Lutz, the Brazilian feminist who fought tirelessly for women's suffrage.

content.text: More Than Just a Scientist
When we hear the word feminist, we often imagine activists holding signs, giving speeches, or standing in the middle of a protest. But Bertha Lutz’s story looks a little different.

Born on August 2, 1894, in São Paulo, Brazil, Bertha Lutz was a scientist, diplomat, and one of the most important figures in Brazil’s fight for women’s rights. And honestly, what makes her interesting is not just what she achieved, but how many different things she managed to do.
She studied science, worked as a biologist, entered politics, and spent years fighting for something that today might seem obvious: women having the right to vote.
A Scientist Who Wanted More
Bertha studied biology and became a specialist in amphibians. While many women of her time were expected to stay within very traditional roles, she was building a career in science.
But science wasn’t the only thing she cared about.

After studying in Europe, Bertha returned to Brazil and became increasingly involved in the women’s rights movement. In 1919, she helped create the Brazilian Federation for Women’s Progress, an organization that pushed for women’s political and social rights.
At the time, women in Brazil couldn’t simply walk into a voting booth and have their voices counted. So Bertha decided that this needed to change.
“Why Shouldn’t Women Vote?”
This is probably my favorite part of her story.
Sometimes, the biggest changes begin with a question that sounds almost too simple.
Why shouldn’t women vote?
Why shouldn’t women study?
Why shouldn’t women have careers?
Why shouldn’t women have a say in the decisions that affect their lives?
Bertha kept asking questions like these and then actually did something about the answers.

She became involved in politics and helped advocate for women’s suffrage for years. Her efforts contributed to Brazil recognizing women’s right to vote in 1932. It wasn’t an overnight victory. It took years of organizing, campaigning, writing, speaking, and refusing to give up
She Wasn’t Waiting For Permission
What I find inspiring about Bertha Lutz is that she didn’t choose just one identity.

She was a scientist and an activist. A diplomat and a feminist. She could spend one part of her life studying biology and another fighting for political rights. And I think that’s something young women today can relate to.

We’re constantly told to choose one thing. Pick one career. Pick one passion. Have one clear plan for your future. But Bertha’s life shows that you don’t necessarily have to fit into one box. You can be interested in science and politics. You can care about your career and social change. You can be ambitious and still want to make things better for other people.
Why Remember Bertha Lutz?
Bertha Lutz died in 1976, but the changes she fought for didn’t disappear with her.
Today, women voting in Brazil is completely normal. It’s easy to forget that there was a time when it wasn’t.
That’s probably the strange thing about progress. Once something becomes normal, we forget how impossible it might have seemed before.

Bertha Lutz lived in a time when women were often told what they couldn’t do. Instead of accepting those limits, she spent her life testing them. And maybe that’s the part of her story worth remembering most.
Credits
• Photo Source: UN Geneva

title: The Day Women Finally Got a Vote
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Learn about the 19th Amendment and the fight for women's suffrage in the United States.

content.text: It Was Never Just About Voting

Imagine living in a country where you have to follow its laws, pay taxes, work, raise a family, and deal with decisions made by politicians but you have no right to choose those politicians yourself. Today, that sounds unfair almost immediately. But for American women, this was normal for a very long time.

On August 18, 1920, the 19th Amendment was ratified, officially recognizing that the right to vote could not be denied on the basis of sex. After decades of protests, campaigns, speeches, petitions, and organizing, women had finally reached a moment they had been fighting for.

But the amendment didn’t appear out of nowhere. Women had been demanding the right to vote since the 19th century. At the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, activists openly discussed women’s political rights at a time when even suggesting that women should participate in politics was controversial. Generation after generation continued the fight, even though many of them would never live to see the amendment become law.

That part makes me think about how strange progress can be. We usually learn history through dates: 1848, 1920, 1965. But behind every date are people who spent years working toward something they might never personally experience. Imagine fighting for a change and knowing that you might not be there when it finally happens. You still keep going because you believe someone else should have the opportunity.
1920 Was A Victory, But It Wasn’t The End

There is also something important that often gets left out when we talk about the 19th Amendment. Saying that it gave women the right to vote can make it sound like every woman in America suddenly walked into a polling station in 1920 and voted freely. That wasn’t what happened.

Black women, Indigenous women, Asian American women, and other women of color continued facing laws, discrimination, intimidation, and other barriers that made voting difficult or impossible in many places. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 became another major step toward protecting voting rights.

So August 18, 1920 was a huge moment, but it wasn’t the finish line. And I actually think that’s an important part of understanding history. We sometimes want one perfect moment where everything suddenly becomes fair, but real change doesn’t work like that. A law can change in one day, while people’s attitudes and systems can take decades to catch up.
Why Does It Still Matter?
For me, the most interesting thing about the 19th Amendment isn’t simply that women were finally allowed to vote. It’s the fact that something that once seemed impossible eventually became normal.

Most of us don’t wake up thinking about how unusual it is that we can participate in elections. We just see voting as one of those things that exists. But there was a time when an entire half of the population was told that their voice didn’t belong in politics.
The women who fought for suffrage didn’t know exactly when they would win. They only knew that they wanted something different from what existed around them. And they kept pushing for it anyway.

Maybe that’s what makes August 18, 1920 worth remembering. Not because one amendment solved everything, but because it shows that laws and traditions are not automatically permanent just because they’ve existed for a long time.
Sometimes, the things we consider completely normal today exist because someone before us looked at the world and thought, “This isn’t fair.”
And then decided not to stop there.
Credits
• Photo Source: Gale

title: When Colombian Women Finally Got to Vote
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Learn about the journey of Colombian women in their fight for the right to vote and the impact of their struggle.

content.text: A Right That Took Years

For a long time, Colombian women could live in the same country, follow the same laws, work, study, and care about what was happening in their communities, but they still couldn’t participate in one of the most basic parts of politics: voting. That changed on August 25, 1954, when Colombia’s National Constituent Assembly recognized women’s political rights. It might sound like just another historical date, but at the time, it meant that women were finally being recognized as political citizens, not just as people affected by political decisions.

What makes this story interesting is that the change didn’t happen overnight. Women had been pushing for greater rights for years, and even after 1954, they still had to wait to actually use their new political right. Their first national vote came in 1957, when Colombian women participated in a referendum for the first time. More than a million women went to the polls, turning what had once been impossible into something real.
Imagine Your First Vote

I sometimes wonder what it must have felt like to vote for the first time when your mother, grandmother, and generations of women before you had never been able to do it. Today, voting can feel like a normal part of growing up. We learn about elections, political parties, and governments at school, and eventually voting becomes something adults simply do. But for these women, entering a polling place in 1957 meant stepping into something completely new.

They weren’t suddenly given opinions that day. They had always had opinions about their country and what should change. The difference was that now those opinions could actually be represented through a vote. And I think that’s an important distinction. Giving someone the right to vote isn’t really giving them a voice, women already had voices. It is giving that voice a place in the political system.
Why We Should Still Remember It

The story of Colombian women’s suffrage also reminds us that progress is usually much slower than we imagine. We look back to 1954 and think, Of course women should have been allowed to vote. But at the time, it was a major political and social change. And even after women gained the right, equality didn’t suddenly appear everywhere.

Still, August 25 remains an important date because it marked the moment when Colombia officially recognized that women belonged in its political life. Three years later, women actually went to the polls and made history themselves.

Today, it is easy to take that right for granted. But maybe that’s exactly why we should remember how it began. Before something becomes normal, there is usually a moment when it was new, uncertain, and even controversial.
For Colombian women, that moment began in 1954 and in 1957, they finally got to make their voices count.
Credits
• Photo Source: Columbia One

title: Women’s Equality Day: Is Equality Ever Finished?
author: Zhanel Bakhmanova
description: Women’s Equality Day is not just a celebration of the past, but a reminder that the fight for equality is ongoing.

content.text: Why August 26 Matters
What if a day celebrating equality was actually created to remind us that the fight for equality isn’t over?

Every year on August 26, the United States celebrates Women’s Equality Day. The date marks the ratification of the 19th Amendment in 1920, which recognized women’s right to vote. More than fifty years later, in 1973, Congress officially designated August 26 as Women’s Equality Day.

At first, it might sound like a celebration of something that happened a long time ago. Women can vote, women can study, work, run for office, and build careers. So why do we still need a day dedicated to equality?
I think that’s what makes this day interesting.
One Amendment Isn't Enough
When we learn about the 19th Amendment, it’s easy to imagine that everything changed overnight. Women won the right to vote, everyone celebrated, and the problem was solved.
But history is rarely that simple.

The amendment was a huge achievement, but it didn’t mean that every woman suddenly experienced equality. Many women of color continued to face discrimination and barriers that prevented them from fully exercising their voting rights. The struggle for equal rights continued long after 1920, and in many ways, it is still continuing today.
That’s why I don’t think Women’s Equality Day should be seen only as a celebration of the past. It is also a reminder to look at the present.
Equality Isn't A Finish Line
One thing I find interesting about equality is that we often talk about it like it’s a destination. As if one day we will finally arrive at “perfect equality” and never have to think about it again.
But society doesn’t really work that way.

The issues women face change with time. The things that were considered impossible for women 100 years ago might seem completely normal today, while completely new challenges appear for the next generation.
And maybe that’s why remembering history matters. If we forget how hard previous generations had to fight for rights that now feel obvious, we can easily start taking them for granted.

I can vote today without thinking about the women who spent decades demanding that right. I can study, choose a career, have ambitions, and imagine a future for myself without wondering whether society will allow me to do those things simply because I’m a girl.
But someone had to fight for that possibility first.
So, What Are We Celebrating?
For me, Women’s Equality Day isn’t about saying that everything is perfect now. It is about recognizing how far women have come while understanding that progress doesn’t mean the story is finished.
August 26 connects the past with the present. It reminds us of the women who demanded a voice in 1920, but it also asks what we are going to do with the opportunities they helped create.
Because equality isn’t something one generation can achieve and then hand over as a finished project.
Every generation gets to decide what it wants to change.
And maybe that’s the real meaning of Women’s Equality Day: not just looking back at how far women have come, but asking ourselves how much further we can go.
